chapter_note.about: This chapter is about arrows and the shadows they cast. The dot product measures how much two arrows agree and gives orthogonality. Projection finds the closest point on a line or a plane, and its matrix is idempotent and symmetric with eigenvalues 0 and 1. Orthogonal matrices keep every length. Block matrices and quadratic forms finish the chapter. GATE rewards reading rank, null space, trace and eigenvalues straight from $P^2=P$, without computing the matrix.
chapter_note.simple: A projection is the shadow of an arrow on a floor. If you squash an arrow to its shadow, squashing it again changes nothing. Arrows lying on the floor keep their size and arrows pointing straight up vanish, so the only stretch factors are 1 and 0. The dot product tells you whether two arrows meet at a right angle. Rotations and mirror flips keep every length. A quadratic form turns an arrow into one number, and for arrows of length 1 that number stays between the smallest and the largest stretch factor of the balanced version of the grid.

cards.title: Dot product and orthogonality
cards.simple: Think of two arrows drawn from the same point. The dot product tells you how much they point the same way. Same direction gives a big positive number, a perfect right angle gives exactly zero, and opposite directions give a negative number. You find it by multiplying the matching numbers of the two arrows and adding them up. The dot of an arrow with itself is its length squared. In exam words: $x^Ty=\sum x_iy_i$, $x\perp y$ exactly when $x^Ty=0$, and $\|x\|^2=x^Tx$.
cards.idea: The **dot product** $x^Ty$ multiplies matching entries and adds them. It measures how much two arrows point the same way. When it is zero the arrows meet at a right angle, and we call them **orthogonal**. The dot of an arrow with itself gives its length squared.
cards.definition:
$$x^Ty=\sum_i x_iy_i=\|x\|\|y\|\cos\theta,\qquad \|x\|^2=x^Tx$$

Here $x,y$ are vectors of the same length, $\theta$ is the angle between them, and $\|x\|$ is the length of $x$. Then $x\perp y$ means $x^Ty=0$. A **unit vector** has $\|u\|=1$, and dividing any non-zero $x$ by $\|x\|$ gives one.
cards.intuition_full: Write $x^Ty=\|x\|\|y\|\cos\theta$. Both lengths are positive, so the sign of the dot product is the sign of $\cos\theta$. Positive: the angle is under $90^\circ$ and the arrows lean the same way. Zero: exactly $90^\circ$. Negative: they lean opposite ways. This is why the single number $x^Ty=0$ is a complete test for perpendicular, even in dimensions where we cannot draw a picture. Setting $y=x$ gives $\cos\theta=1$, so $x^Tx=\|x\|^2$ is a sum of squares, which is Pythagoras. Normalising (dividing by the length) keeps the direction and sets the length to 1. Two non-zero vectors give the same unit vector exactly when one is a positive multiple of the other.

examples.setup: Let $x=(3,1)$ and $y=(-1,3)$. Are they orthogonal? Find $\|x\|$ and the unit vector along $x$.
steps: Draw $x=(3,1)$ and $y=(-1,3)$ from the origin.
A zero dot product means $\cos\theta=0$, so the angle is $90^\circ$ and $x\perp y$.
Length: $x^Tx=9+1=10$, so $\|x\|=\sqrt{10}\approx3.16$.
Unit vector: $u=x/\|x\|=(3,1)/\sqrt{10}\approx(0.95,\,0.32)$, which has length 1.
Orthogonal means the dot product is exactly 0. Compute each one.
examples.answer: P, Q and S are orthogonal. R is not (its dot product is 4). Only the dot product decides; a picture or equal lengths prove nothing.

examples.setup: True or false: if $x^Ty=0$ then $x=0$ or $y=0$. Is the zero vector orthogonal to $(1,2,3)$?
steps: The zero vector: $0^T(1,2,3)=0$, so it is orthogonal to every vector.
Now take $x=(1,2)$ and $y=(2,-1)$. Both are non-zero, yet $x^Ty=2-2=0$.
So the statement is false. Unlike two numbers multiplied together, a zero dot product does not force a zero factor.
The one product that does force it is $x^Tx=\sum x_i^2$: it is 0 only when every entry is 0.
examples.answer: False. $(1,2)\perp(2,-1)$ with both non-zero. Only $x^Tx=0$ forces $x=0$.

cards.why: Orthogonality and length are the basic tools of the whole chapter: projections, orthogonal matrices and quadratic forms all start from $x^Ty$. In GATE: test orthogonality, find the unknown entry that makes a dot product zero, or normalise a vector.
how: Multiply matching entries and add them. That is $x^Ty$.
For orthogonality, set $x^Ty=0$ and solve for the unknown.
For length, compute $x^Tx$ and take the square root.
For a unit vector, divide by $\|x\|$.
cards.mistake: Checking only that lengths match or that the picture looks perpendicular. Orthogonal means $x^Ty=0$ exactly. Another slip is forgetting the square root, writing $\|x\|=x^Tx$ instead of $\sqrt{x^Tx}$.
edge_cases: The zero vector is orthogonal to every vector.
$x^Tx=0$ only for $x=0$.
Non-zero orthogonal vectors are always linearly independent.
Scaling a vector never changes whether it is orthogonal to another.
connections: The next card projects one vector onto another using exactly $x^Ty$ and $x^Tx$.
Orthogonal matrices (card 7) are matrices whose columns are orthogonal unit vectors.

cards.title: Projection onto a vector
cards.simple: Imagine a lamp straight above a rod lying on the table. Hold an arrow in the air and look at its shadow on the rod. The shadow is the projection. To find how long the shadow is, compare how much your arrow agrees with the rod (the dot product) with the rod's own length squared. That ratio says how many rod-lengths you walk along the rod. The leftover piece, from the tip of the shadow up to your arrow, meets the rod at a right angle. In exam words: $\operatorname{proj}_ab=\frac{a^Tb}{a^Ta}a$, and the residual $b-p$ is orthogonal to $a$.
cards.idea: The **projection** of $b$ onto the line through $a$ is the point of that line closest to $b$. It is a multiple of $a$, and the leftover $b-p$ is perpendicular to $a$. That one condition decides the multiple.
cards.definition:
$$p=\operatorname{proj}_a b=\frac{a^Tb}{a^Ta}\,a,\qquad P=\frac{aa^T}{a^Ta}$$

$a\ne0$ gives the direction of the line, $b$ is the vector being projected, and $P$ is the matrix that does it ($p=Pb$). The **residual** is $r=b-p$, and it satisfies $a^Tr=0$.
cards.intuition_full: Write $p=ca$ for an unknown number $c$. We want $b-ca$ perpendicular to $a$, so $a^T(b-ca)=0$. Expand: $a^Tb-c\,a^Ta=0$, so $c=a^Tb/a^Ta$. Each part has a job. $a^Tb$ measures how much $b$ agrees with $a$. $a^Ta$ rescales by the length of $a$ squared, so a longer $a$ does not change the answer. A second picture is the shortest distance from a point to a line: the shortest path hits the line at a right angle, and its foot is $p$. Pythagoras then gives $\|b\|^2=\|p\|^2+\|r\|^2$. If $a$ is a unit vector, $a^Ta=1$ and the formula simplifies to $p=(a^Tb)a$.

examples.setup: Project $b=(2,3)$ onto the line through $a=(3,1)$. Find $p$ and the residual.
steps: Draw $b=(2,3)$ and the line through $a=(3,1)$. We want the point of the line closest to $b$.
Compute $a^Tb=3\cdot2+1\cdot3=9$ and $a^Ta=9+1=10$.
Check: $a^Tr=3(-0.7)+1(2.1)=0$. The residual is perpendicular to the line, so $p$ is the closest point.

examples.setup: Let $a=(1,1,2)$ and $b=(2,0,1)$. Find $p=\operatorname{proj}_ab$, $\|p\|^2$ and $\|b-p\|^2$.
steps: $a^Tb=1\cdot2+1\cdot0+2\cdot1=4$ and $a^Ta=1+1+4=6$.
$p=\tfrac46\,a=\tfrac23(1,1,2)=(\tfrac23,\tfrac23,\tfrac43)$.
$\|p\|^2=\tfrac49+\tfrac49+\tfrac{16}9=\tfrac{24}9=\tfrac83$. Shortcut: $\|p\|^2=(a^Tb)^2/a^Ta=16/6=\tfrac83$.
Pythagoras: $\|b-p\|^2=\|b\|^2-\|p\|^2=5-\tfrac83=\tfrac73$.
examples.answer: $p=(\tfrac23,\tfrac23,\tfrac43)$, $\|p\|^2=\tfrac83$ and $\|b-p\|^2=\tfrac73$.

examples.setup: Project $b=(3,-2)$ onto $a=(0,2)$, and then onto $a'=(0,5)$. What do you notice?
steps: With $a=(0,2)$: $a^Tb=0\cdot3+2\cdot(-2)=-4$ and $a^Ta=4$, so the multiplier is $-1$.
$p=-1\cdot(0,2)=(0,-2)$. It points opposite to $a$, because $b$ leans away from $a$ (negative dot product).
Same $p$. The projection depends on the line, not on how long a vector we pick to describe it.
examples.answer: $p=(0,-2)$ both times. A negative multiplier is fine, and rescaling $a$ changes nothing.

cards.why: Projection is the closest-point operation behind least squares and the projection matrices of the next cards. In GATE: compute $p$, one entry of $P$, or the length of the residual.
how: Compute $a^Tb$ and $a^Ta$.

The residual is $r=b-p$.

cards.mistake: Forgetting to divide by $a^Ta$, or dividing by $\|a\|$ (not squared) when $a$ is not a unit vector. Also projecting onto $b$ instead of onto $a$. The order matters: $\operatorname{proj}_ab\ne\operatorname{proj}_ba$.
edge_cases: If $b\perp a$, then $a^Tb=0$ and $p=0$.
If $b$ is a multiple of $a$, then $p=b$ and $r=0$.
A negative $a^Tb$ gives a $p$ pointing opposite to $a$.
Rescaling $a$ changes neither $p$ nor $P$.
connections: The matrix $P=aa^T/a^Ta$ is the subject of the next card.
Least squares (card 6) is the same idea with a whole subspace in place of a line.

check.a: The zero vector. $b$ is perpendicular to the line.

cards.title: Projection matrix properties
cards.simple: A projection is like the shadow of an arrow on the floor when the sun is straight overhead. Squash an arrow to its shadow, and if you squash the shadow again nothing changes, because it is already flat. Arrows lying on the floor stay exactly as they are (stretch 1), and arrows pointing straight up vanish (stretch 0). So the only stretch factors are 0 and 1. In exam words: a projection matrix has $P^2=P$, $P^T=P$, eigenvalues 0 and 1, and $\operatorname{tr}P=\operatorname{rank}P$.
cards.idea: A matrix $P$ that **projects** squashes every vector onto a subspace. Projecting a second time changes nothing, so $P^2=P$. Vectors already in the subspace stay put (eigenvalue 1), and vectors perpendicular to it vanish (eigenvalue 0).
cards.definition:
An orthogonal projection matrix satisfies:

- $P^2=P$ (idempotent) and $P^T=P$ (symmetric).
- Its eigenvalues are only $1$ and $0$. The number of 1s is $\operatorname{rank}P$.
- $\operatorname{tr}P=\operatorname{rank}P=\dim U$ for the subspace $U$ it projects onto.
- $\det P=0$ unless $P=I$.

Conversely, $P^2=P$ and $P^T=P$ together mean that $P$ is an orthogonal projection.
cards.intuition_full: Start from $P^2=P$. If $Pv=\lambda v$, then $P^2v=\lambda^2v$, and also $P^2v=Pv=\lambda v$. So $\lambda^2=\lambda$ and $\lambda$ is 0 or 1. The eigenvectors for 1 fill the subspace $U$, since $P$ fixes them. The eigenvectors for 0 fill the perpendicular complement, since $P$ sends them to zero. Because the eigenvalues are only 0 and 1, adding them counts the 1s, which is $\dim U$. So $\operatorname{tr}P=\dim U=\operatorname{rank}P$. Symmetry says the two eigenspaces are perpendicular. Powers collapse: $P^3=P\cdot P^2=P$, so every power of $P$ is $P$. A single zero eigenvalue kills the determinant, so $\det P=0$ for any projection onto a proper subspace.

examples.setup: $P=\dfrac{aa^T}{a^Ta}$ with $a=(3,1)$. Show that $P^2=P$ and find the eigenvalues and the trace.
steps: $aa^T=\begin{pmatrix}9&3\\3&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $a^Ta=10$, so $P=\begin{pmatrix}0.9&0.3\\0.3&0.1\end{pmatrix}$. It is symmetric.
$Pa=(0.9\cdot3+0.3\cdot1,\ 0.3\cdot3+0.1\cdot1)=(3,1)=a$. A vector on the line stays put: eigenvalue 1.
Take $w=(-1,3)$, which is perpendicular to $a$. $Pw=(0.9(-1)+0.3\cdot3,\ 0.3(-1)+0.1\cdot3)=(0,0)$. Eigenvalue 0.
$\operatorname{tr}P=0.9+0.1=1=1+0$. The trace is the sum of the eigenvalues, so $\operatorname{tr}P=\operatorname{rank}P=1$.
$P^2=P$: for $b=(2,3)$, $Pb=(2.7,0.9)$, and projecting again gives $P(2.7,0.9)=(2.7,0.9)$. Nothing changes the second time.
examples.answer: $P^2=P$, the eigenvalues are 1 and 0, and $\operatorname{tr}P=\operatorname{rank}P=1$.

examples.setup: $P$ is the orthogonal projection of $\mathbb R^6$ onto a 4-dimensional subspace. Which are true? A: $\operatorname{tr}P=4$. B: $\det P=1$. C: $P^3=P$. D: $\dim\ker P=4$.
steps: $P^2=P$ and $P^T=P$, so the eigenvalues are 1 (four times) and 0 (twice).
A: $\operatorname{tr}P=4\cdot1+2\cdot0=4$. True.
B: $\det P=1^4\cdot0^2=0$, not 1. False.
C: $P^3=P\cdot P^2=P\cdot P=P$. True.
D: $\dim\ker P=6-\operatorname{rank}P=6-4=2$, not 4. False.
examples.answer: A and C are true. B and D are false.

examples.setup: $P$ projects $\mathbb R^3$ onto a plane. Is $2P$ a projection? What are its eigenvalues and its trace?
steps: Test the defining rule: $(2P)^2=4P^2=4P$.
A projection would need $(2P)^2=2P$, so $4P=2P$, which forces $P=0$. The test fails.
The eigenvalues of $2P$ are twice those of $P$: $2,2,0$.
The trace is 4 but the rank is 2. For a projection the trace equals the rank, so this fails as well.
examples.answer: $2P$ is not a projection (eigenvalues $2,2,0$; trace $4\ne$ rank $2$). The eigenvalues must be exactly 0 and 1.

cards.why: Almost every projection question is a true-or-false on these properties, answered without computing anything. In GATE: statements about rank, null space, trace and powers of a projection (2024 DA Q49, 2025 DA Q50, 2026 DA Q52).
how: Confirm $P^2=P$ and $P^T=P$, or read it from the description.
List the eigenvalues: 1 with multiplicity $\dim U$, 0 with multiplicity $n-\dim U$.
Read the trace, rank, determinant and nullity from that list.
Powers: $P^k=P$ for every $k\ge1$.
A scaled or shifted $P$, such as $2P$ or $I+P$, is no longer a projection.
cards.mistake: Using $\det P=1$, or thinking $P$ is invertible. Every projection onto a proper subspace has a zero eigenvalue, so $\det P=0$ and $P$ is singular. Also treating $2P$ or $P+I$ as projections.
edge_cases: $P=I$ projects onto the whole space: all eigenvalues 1, $\det=1$.
$P=0$ projects onto $\{0\}$: all eigenvalues 0 and rank 0.
$\operatorname{tr}P=\operatorname{rank}P$ is always a whole number.
The sum of two projections is usually not a projection.
connections: Idempotent matrices (next card) drop the symmetry and keep eigenvalues 0 and 1.
The eigenvalue chapter lists rank-1 and projection matrices as the shapes with easy eigenvalues.

check.a: 5. For a projection the trace equals the rank.

cards.title: Idempotent matrices
cards.simple: Idempotent just means 'doing it twice is the same as doing it once', like pressing 'sort' on a list that is already sorted, or flattening a pancake that is already flat. A matrix with $A\cdot A=A$ behaves this way. It can only stretch arrows by 0 (squash) or 1 (leave alone). It may squash arrows at a slant, like a shadow made by a lamp that is not overhead. Then it is still idempotent, but it is not symmetric. In exam words: $A^2=A$ gives eigenvalues 0 and 1 and $\operatorname{rank}A=\operatorname{tr}A$, and $A$ need not be symmetric.
cards.idea: A matrix is **idempotent** if applying it twice does the same as applying it once: $A^2=A$. Its eigenvalues can only be 0 and 1, and its rank equals its trace. It does not have to be symmetric. A non-symmetric one projects along a slant instead of at a right angle.
cards.definition:
$$A^2=A\ \Longrightarrow\ \lambda\in\{0,1\},\qquad \operatorname{rank}A=\operatorname{tr}A$$

$A$ is square. It projects onto its column space $\operatorname{col}A$ along its null space $\ker A$. It is an **orthogonal** projection exactly when those two subspaces are perpendicular, which happens exactly when $A^T=A$.
cards.intuition_full: The same algebra as for projections works without symmetry: $\lambda^2=\lambda$ gives $\lambda\in\{0,1\}$. Every vector $v$ splits as $Av+(v-Av)$. cards.title: Complement and null space
cards.simple: Take a shadow on the floor. Every arrow splits into two parts: the shadow, and the bit that sticks straight up. Together they rebuild the arrow. The projection keeps the shadow and kills the up-part, so everything that points straight up is sent to zero. Those vanishing arrows are the null space. The matrix $I-P$ does the opposite: it keeps the up-part and kills the shadow. In exam words: $b=Pb+(I-P)b$, $\ker P=U^\perp$, and $I-P$ projects onto $U^\perp$.
cards.idea: Every vector splits into a part inside the subspace $U$ and a part perpendicular to it: $b=Pb+(I-P)b$. The matrix $P$ keeps the first part and kills the second. So everything perpendicular to $U$ is sent to zero: that set is the **null space** of $P$. The matrix $I-P$ does the opposite.
cards.definition:
$$b=Pb+(I-P)b,\qquad \ker P=U^\perp,\qquad \operatorname{col}(I-P)=U^\perp$$

$U$ is the subspace projected onto, and $U^\perp$ is the set of all vectors perpendicular to $U$. Dimensions: $\dim\ker P=n-\operatorname{rank}P=n-\dim U$. $I-P$ is also an orthogonal projection, with $\operatorname{tr}(I-P)=n-\operatorname{tr}P$.
cards.intuition_full: The two pieces are perpendicular, so they do not overlap and nothing is lost: the pair $(Pb,(I-P)b)$ rebuilds $b$ exactly. If $b$ already lies in $U$, then $Pb=b$ and the leftover is 0. If $b\perp U$, then $Pb=0$, so $b$ is in the null space. These are the only two ways $P$ can act, which is why the eigenvalues are 1 (on $U$) and 0 (on $U^\perp$). Count dimensions: $U$ has $\dim U$ free directions, $U^\perp$ has the remaining $n-\dim U$, and together they fill $\mathbb R^n$. The complement $I-P$ swaps the roles. It keeps $U^\perp$ and kills $U$, so $\ker(I-P)=U$. The ranks of $P$ and $I-P$ always add up to $n$.

examples.setup: Let $U$ be the line through $a=(1,2)$ and let $b=(3,1)$. Split $b$ into a part in $U$ and a part in $U^\perp$.
steps: Project: $a^Tb=1\cdot3+2\cdot1=5$ and $a^Ta=1+4=5$, so $Pb=1\cdot a=(1,2)$.
The leftover is $(I-P)b=b-Pb=(3,1)-(1,2)=(2,-1)$.
Check that it is perpendicular to $a$: $a\cdot(2,-1)=2-2=0$. So the leftover lies in $U^\perp$.
So $b=(1,2)+(2,-1)$: one piece in $U$ and one in $U^\perp$. Together they rebuild $b$.
$P$ sends all of $U^\perp$ to 0, so $\ker P=U^\perp=\operatorname{span}(2,-1)$ and $\dim\ker P=2-1=1$.

steps: $\operatorname{rank}P=\dim U=4$.
$\ker P=U^\perp$, so $\dim\ker P=9-4=5$.
$I-P$ projects onto $U^\perp$, so $\operatorname{rank}(I-P)=5$ and $\operatorname{tr}(I-P)=5$ (trace equals rank).
$\ker(I-P)$ is the set of $v$ with $Pv=v$, which is $U$ itself, so its dimension is 4.
examples.answer: $5,\ 5,\ 4,\ 5$, in that order.

examples.setup: $M=I-\tfrac14\mathbf 1\mathbf 1^T$ on $\mathbb R^4$ (the centering matrix). Find $\operatorname{rank}M$, $\ker M$, and $Mx$ for $x=(2,4,6,12)$.
steps: $\mathbf1^T\mathbf1=4$, so $P=\tfrac14\mathbf1\mathbf1^T$ projects onto the line spanned by $\mathbf1=(1,1,1,1)$. Then $M=I-P$.
So $M$ projects onto $U^\perp$, the vectors whose entries add to 0. That is 3-dimensional, so $\operatorname{rank}M=3=\operatorname{tr}M$.
$Mx=x-(\text{mean of }x)\,\mathbf1$. The mean of $x$ is $24/4=6$, so $Mx=(-4,-2,0,6)$.
$\ker M=\operatorname{span}(\mathbf1)$, the constant vectors, so $\dim\ker M=1$.
examples.answer: $\operatorname{rank}M=3$, $\ker M=\operatorname{span}(\mathbf1)$ and $Mx=(-4,-2,0,6)$, whose entries sum to 0.

cards.title: Projection onto a subspace
cards.simple: Now the floor is a whole flat sheet instead of a single rod. To find the shadow of a point on the sheet, you drop a straight line from the point down onto it, and the landing spot is the closest point on the sheet. To compute it, you say: the landing spot is some mix of the sheet's direction arrows, with unknown amounts, and the leftover must be at a right angle to every direction arrow. That gives a small set of equations, called the normal equations. If the direction arrows already stand at right angles and have length 1, the amounts are just dot products. In exam words: $P=A(A^TA)^{-1}A^T$, and $P=QQ^T$ when the columns are orthonormal.
cards.idea: To project $b$ onto the **column space** of $A$ (all mixes of its columns), write the answer as $p=Ax$ and demand that the leftover $b-Ax$ is perpendicular to every column. That gives $A^TAx=A^Tb$, the **normal equations**. If the columns are orthonormal, it collapses to $x=Q^Tb$.
cards.definition:
$$A^TAx=A^Tb,\qquad p=Ax,\qquad P=A(A^TA)^{-1}A^T$$

$A$ is $n\times k$ with independent columns, $x$ holds the amount of each column, and $p=Pb$ is the projection of $b$ onto $\operatorname{col}A$. If $Q$ has orthonormal columns, then $Q^TQ=I$ and $P=QQ^T$.
cards.intuition_full: The condition 'leftover is perpendicular to every column' is $A^T(b-Ax)=0$, one dot product per column. Rearranged, it is $A^TAx=A^Tb$. The matrix $A^TA$ holds all the dot products between the columns, and $A^Tb$ holds the dot products of $b$ with each column. $A^TA$ is invertible exactly when the columns are independent. Then $x=(A^TA)^{-1}A^Tb$, and $p=Ax$ gives $P$ in one line. With orthonormal columns $A^TA=I$, so $x=Q^Tb$: each amount is just $q_i^Tb$, and $p=\sum(q_i^Tb)\,q_i$ is a sum of line projections. This is also least squares: $p$ is the closest point of $\operatorname{col}A$ to $b$, so $x$ minimises $\|b-Ax\|$. The earlier rules still hold: $\operatorname{tr}P=\operatorname{rank}A=k$.

examples.setup: Project $b=(3,0,3)$ onto the column space of $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$.
steps: The columns are $(1,1,0)$ and $(0,1,1)$. We want $p=Ax$ with $b-Ax$ perpendicular to both columns.
$A^TA=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$, the dot products of the columns.
$A^Tb=\begin{pmatrix}1\cdot3+1\cdot0+0\cdot3\\0\cdot3+1\cdot0+1\cdot3\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\3\end{pmatrix}$.
Solve $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}x=\begin{pmatrix}3\\3\end{pmatrix}$ to get $x=(1,1)$.
Check: $r=b-p=(2,-2,2)$ and $A^Tr=(2-2,\ -2+2)=(0,0)$. The residual is perpendicular to both columns.

examples.setup: $q_1=\tfrac12(1,1,1,1)$ and $q_2=\tfrac12(1,-1,1,-1)$ are orthonormal, and $P$ projects onto their span. For $b=(4,2,6,0)$ find $Pb$, $\|Pb\|^2$ and $\|b-Pb\|^2$.
steps: The columns are orthonormal: $q_1^Tq_1=\tfrac14\cdot4=1$, $q_2^Tq_2=1$ and $q_1^Tq_2=\tfrac14(1-1+1-1)=0$. So $Q^TQ=I$ and $P=QQ^T$.
Coordinates: $q_1^Tb=\tfrac12(4+2+6+0)=6$ and $q_2^Tb=\tfrac12(4-2+6-0)=4$.
$\|Pb\|^2=6^2+4^2=52$ (the squares of the coordinates). Also $\|b\|^2=16+4+36+0=56$.
Pythagoras: $\|b-Pb\|^2=56-52=4$. Direct check: $b-Pb=(-1,1,1,-1)$, and its squares add to 4.

cards.title: Orthogonal matrices
cards.simple: A rotation or a mirror flip moves arrows around without stretching them. Lay a ruler on a table and turn the table: the ruler is just as long as before, and the angle between two rulers does not change. A matrix that does this is called orthogonal. Its columns are arrows of length 1, at right angles to each other. In exam words: $Q^TQ=I$, $\|Qx\|=\|x\|$, $\det Q=\pm1$, and every eigenvalue has $|\lambda|=1$.
cards.idea: An **orthogonal matrix** $Q$ is a rotation or a mirror flip. Its columns are perpendicular arrows of length 1. It moves arrows around without stretching them, so lengths and angles stay the same. That is why its determinant is $\pm1$ and all its eigenvalues have size 1.
cards.definition:
$$Q^TQ=I\ \Longleftrightarrow\ Q^{-1}=Q^T$$

$Q$ is square. Consequences: $\|Qx\|=\|x\|$, $(Qx)^T(Qy)=x^Ty$, $\det Q=\pm1$ ($+1$ for a rotation, $-1$ for a reflection), every eigenvalue has $|\lambda|=1$, and all singular values equal 1.
cards.intuition_full: The entry $(Q^TQ)_{ij}$ is the dot product of column $i$ with column $j$. Asking for $Q^TQ=I$ says every column has length 1 (the diagonal) and different columns are perpendicular (the off-diagonal). Then $\|Qx\|^2=x^TQ^TQx=x^Tx$, so lengths are kept. Dot products are kept too, so angles are kept. A map that keeps all lengths cannot squash space, so $|\det Q|=1$. Its eigenvalues, possibly complex, also have size 1, since $|\lambda|\|v\|=\|Qv\|=\|v\|$. The sign of the determinant separates rotations from reflections: a rotation can be turned smoothly back into the identity, and a mirror flip cannot. Inverting is free, because $Q^{-1}=Q^T$. A question asking for an entry of $Q^{-1}$ just wants the transposed entry.

examples.setup: $Q=\begin{pmatrix}0.6&-0.8\\0.8&0.6\end{pmatrix}$. Show that $Q$ is orthogonal, and find $\|Qx\|$ for $x=(5,0)$.
steps: So $Q^TQ=I$ and $Q$ is orthogonal.
Lengths: $\|x\|=5$ and $\|Qx\|=\sqrt{9+16}=5$. Unchanged.
$\det Q=0.6\cdot0.6-(-0.8)(0.8)=0.36+0.64=1$, so $Q$ is a rotation. A reflection would have $\det=-1$.
examples.answer: $Q$ is orthogonal, $\|Qx\|=5=\|x\|$ and $\det Q=1$ (a rotation).

examples.setup: $Q=\tfrac13\begin{pmatrix}2&-2&1\\1&2&2\\2&1&-2\end{pmatrix}$ is orthogonal. Find $\det Q$, the entry $(Q^{-1})_{12}$, and $\|Qx\|^2$ for $x=(1,-2,2)$.
steps: Check the columns: $\tfrac13(2,1,2)$, $\tfrac13(-2,2,1)$ and $\tfrac13(1,2,-2)$ each have length $\tfrac13\sqrt9=1$. Their dot products are $\tfrac19(-4+2+2)=0$, $\tfrac19(2+2-4)=0$ and $\tfrac19(-2+4-2)=0$.
$\det Q$ is $\pm1$. Expanding it gives $\det Q=-1$, so this is a reflection-type orthogonal matrix.
$\|Qx\|^2=\|x\|^2=1+4+4=9$. There is no need to multiply.

examples.setup: $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ has perpendicular columns. Is $A$ orthogonal? How do you fix it?
steps: The columns $(1,1)$ and $(1,-1)$ have dot product $1-1=0$, so they are perpendicular.
But each has length $\sqrt2$, not 1. $A^TA=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}=2I\ne I$, so $A$ is not orthogonal.
Divide by $\sqrt2$: $Q=A/\sqrt2$ has unit columns, so $Q^TQ=I$. And $\det Q=\tfrac12(-1-1)=-1$.
examples.answer: $A$ is not orthogonal ($A^TA=2I$ and $\|Ax\|=\sqrt2\|x\|$). $Q=A/\sqrt2$ is orthogonal, with $\det Q=-1$.

cards.title: Partitioned matrices
cards.simple: Imagine cutting a big table of numbers into four smaller tables, like cutting a chocolate bar into four pieces. You can multiply the pieces as if each one were a single number, as long as you keep the order and the sizes match. If one piece in the right corner is all zeros, the big table's determinant is just the product of the determinants of the two diagonal pieces, and the other piece does not matter at all. In exam words: block multiplication follows row-by-column with blocks, and for block triangular $M=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\0&D\end{pmatrix}$ we have $\det M=\det A\cdot\det D$.
cards.idea: You can cut a big matrix into rectangular **blocks** and treat the blocks like single numbers when multiplying. If the matrix is block triangular, with a block of zeros on one side of the diagonal blocks, its determinant is the product of the determinants of the diagonal blocks, and the other block does not matter.
cards.definition:
For $M=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\0&D\end{pmatrix}$ with $A$ and $D$ square:

- $\det M=\det A\cdot\det D$.
- $\operatorname{rank}M\ge\operatorname{rank}A+\operatorname{rank}D$, with equality when $B=0$ (block diagonal).
- Block product: $M^2=\begin{pmatrix}A^2&AB+BD\\0&D^2\end{pmatrix}$.

Block sizes must fit in every product, and the order of the factors matters.
cards.intuition_full: Block multiplication is ordinary row-times-column multiplication done one block at a time: block $(i,j)$ of a product is the sum over $k$ of (block $(i,k)$)(block $(k,j)$). It works because sums of products regroup freely, as long as the shapes fit. For the determinant, expand along the first columns. The zero block means every non-zero term must take its entries from $A$'s rows in those columns, so the determinant factors into $\det A$ times $\det D$. The block $B$ is never multiplied by anything in that expansion, so it is free. Rank behaves differently. A block diagonal matrix splits the rank exactly, but a non-zero $B$ can create extra independent columns, so the rank can be larger than $\operatorname{rank}A+\operatorname{rank}D$.

examples.setup: $M=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&5&6\\1&3&7&8\\0&0&1&2\\0&0&0&3\end{pmatrix}$ is split into $2\times2$ blocks $\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\0&D\end{pmatrix}$. Find $\det M$.
steps: Split $M$ into $2\times2$ blocks: $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$ top-left, $B=\begin{pmatrix}5&6\\7&8\end{pmatrix}$ top-right, a zero block bottom-left, and $D=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$ bottom-right.
The zero block below the diagonal makes $M$ block upper triangular.
$\det A=2\cdot3-1\cdot1=5$.
$\det D=1\cdot3-2\cdot0=3$.
$\det M=\det A\cdot\det D=5\cdot3=15$. The block $B$ plays no part.
examples.answer: $\det M=15$, whatever the entries of $B$ are.

examples.setup: $M=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&1\\0&1&2\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ with $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}$. Use blocks to find $M^2$.
steps: Block product: $M^2=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\0&1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}A^2&AB+B\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$.
$A^2=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$.
$AB=\begin{pmatrix}1\cdot1+1\cdot2\\0\cdot1+1\cdot2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\end{pmatrix}$, so $AB+B=\begin{pmatrix}4\\4\end{pmatrix}$.
Assemble: $M^2=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&4\\0&1&4\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$.
examples.answer: $M^2=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&4\\0&1&4\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$, and $\det M^2=\det(A^2)\cdot1=1$.

examples.setup: $M=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ is viewed as blocks $A=(0)$, $B=(1)$, $D=(0)$. Is $\operatorname{rank}M=\operatorname{rank}A+\operatorname{rank}D$?
steps: $\operatorname{rank}A=0$ and $\operatorname{rank}D=0$, so the sum is 0.
But $M$ has a non-zero entry, so $\operatorname{rank}M=1$.
For block triangular matrices, $\operatorname{rank}M\ge\operatorname{rank}A+\operatorname{rank}D$. Equality is guaranteed only when $B=0$ (block diagonal).
The determinant rule still holds: $\det M=\det A\cdot\det D=0\cdot0=0$.
examples.answer: No: $\operatorname{rank}M=1>0+0$. The determinant factors for block triangular matrices, but the rank need not.

$\det M=\det A\det D$ needs $A$ and $D$ to be square.
The inverse of a block triangular matrix is block triangular, with $A^{-1}$ and $D^{-1}$ on the diagonal.

cards.title: Quadratic forms
cards.simple: A quadratic form turns an arrow into a single number, like squaring a length but with a twist from a matrix. You get it by multiplying out: for the arrow $(x,y)$ you get a mix of $x^2$, $xy$ and $y^2$. The surprise is that only the 'balanced' part of the matrix matters, because the two cross entries always appear together. On arrows of length 1, the number stays between the smallest and largest stretch factors of the balanced matrix. In exam words: $x^TAx=x^T\frac{A+A^T}{2}x$, and on unit vectors it ranges between $\lambda_{\min}$ and $\lambda_{\max}$ of the symmetric part.
cards.idea: A **quadratic form** $x^TAx$ turns a vector into a single number built from squares and cross terms like $x_1x_2$. Only the symmetric part of $A$ matters, because the two off-diagonal entries always show up together. On vectors of length 1, the form ranges from the smallest to the largest eigenvalue of that symmetric part.
cards.definition:
$$x^TAx=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}x_ix_j=x^TSx,\qquad S=\tfrac{A+A^T}{2}$$

$S$ is the symmetric part of $A$. For symmetric $S$ and $x\ne0$: $\lambda_{\min}\le\dfrac{x^TSx}{x^Tx}\le\lambda_{\max}$ (the **Rayleigh quotient**), with equality at the matching eigenvectors. $A$ is **positive definite** if $x^TAx>0$ for all $x\ne0$.
cards.intuition_full: $x^TAx$ is a single number, so it equals its own transpose: $x^TAx=(x^TAx)^T=x^TA^Tx$. Average the two: $x^TAx=x^T\frac{A+A^T}{2}x$. So $a_{12}$ and $a_{21}$ enter only through their sum, and we may replace both by their average without changing the form. Now diagonalise the symmetric part: $S=Q\Lambda Q^T$ with orthonormal eigenvectors. In the coordinates $y=Q^Tx$ the form becomes $\sum\lambda_iy_i^2$, with $\sum y_i^2=1$ for a unit $x$. A weighted average of the $\lambda_i$, with weights $y_i^2$, lies between the smallest and the largest. That is the Rayleigh bound. Positive definite means every $\lambda_i>0$. For a $2\times2$ matrix, test $a_{11}>0$ and $\det>0$. Positive diagonal entries alone are not enough. The eigenvalues of the original non-symmetric $A$ do not matter here.

examples.setup: $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&4\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$ is not symmetric. Evaluate $x^TAx$ at $x=(2,1)$, and find the symmetric $S$ with $x^TAx=x^TSx$.
steps: The cross term $4x_1x_2$ comes from both off-diagonal entries together: $4+0$.
Split it evenly: $S=\tfrac{A+A^T}{2}=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$. Its cross terms are $2x_1x_2+2x_2x_1=4x_1x_2$.
$x^TSx$ at $(2,1)$: $1\cdot4+2\cdot2\cdot(2\cdot1)+3\cdot1=4+8+3=15$. The same value.
examples.answer: $x^TAx=15$ and $S=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$. Only the symmetric part counts.

examples.setup: $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&6\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$. Find the maximum and the minimum of $x^TAx$ over unit vectors $x$.
steps: $x^TAx=2x_1^2+6x_1x_2+2x_2^2$. Only the symmetric part counts.
$S=\tfrac{A+A^T}{2}=\begin{pmatrix}2&3\\3&2\end{pmatrix}$.
Eigenvalues of $S$: trace 4 and determinant $4-9=-5$, so $\lambda^2-4\lambda-5=0$ and $\lambda=5,\ -1$.
On unit vectors, $x^TAx$ ranges over $[-1,\,5]$. Check the maximum at $x=(1,1)/\sqrt2$: $2\cdot\tfrac12+6\cdot\tfrac12+2\cdot\tfrac12=5$.
Trap: the eigenvalues of $A$ itself are 2 and 2. They would give the wrong answer.
examples.answer: Maximum 5 and minimum $-1$: the eigenvalues of $S$, not of $A$.

examples.setup: Is $x^TAx>0$ for every $x\ne0$ when $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&3\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$? Both diagonal entries are positive.
steps: Positive diagonal entries are necessary, but not sufficient.
For a $2\times2$ matrix use the determinant: $\det A=2\cdot4-3\cdot3=-1<0$. So one eigenvalue is negative and $A$ is indefinite.
Find a witness: $x=(3,-2)$ gives $2\cdot9+2\cdot3\cdot(3\cdot(-2))+4\cdot4=18-36+16=-2<0$.
examples.answer: No. $\det A=-1<0$, and $x=(3,-2)$ gives $x^TAx=-2$.

cards.why: Quadratic forms link matrices to optimisation: the sign of the form decides whether a point is a minimum, and the Rayleigh bounds give the maximum over the unit sphere. In GATE: evaluate $x^TAx$, find the symmetric part, find a maximum on unit vectors, or test positive definiteness (2026 DA Q65).
how: Expand $x^TAx$ into $x_i^2$ terms and cross terms.
For a non-symmetric $A$, replace it by $S=(A+A^T)/2$ first.
The maximum and minimum on unit $x$ are the largest and smallest eigenvalues of $S$.
Positive definite: all eigenvalues of $S$ positive (for $2\times2$: $a_{11}>0$ and $\det>0$).
Verify at one test vector.
cards.mistake: Using the eigenvalues of a non-symmetric $A$ for the extremes of $x^TAx$. Only the symmetric part counts. Another slip is judging positive definiteness from the diagonal entries alone.
edge_cases: For $x=0$ the form is 0, and scaling $x$ by $t$ scales the form by $t^2$.
An antisymmetric $A$ ($A^T=-A$) has $x^TAx=0$ for every $x$.
Positive semidefinite allows eigenvalues of 0, so $x^TAx\ge0$.
The Rayleigh bounds are for $x^TSx/x^Tx$, so scale $x$ to unit length first.
connections: Eigenvalue chapter: the Rayleigh quotient card has the same bound.

3. The cross term $4x_1x_2$ comes from both off-diagonal entries together: $4+0$.
4. Split it evenly: $S=\tfrac{A+A^T}{2}=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$. Its cross terms are $2x_1x_2+2x_2x_1=4x_1x_2$.
5. $x^TSx$ at $(2,1)$: $1\cdot4+2\cdot2\cdot(2\cdot1)+3\cdot1=4+8+3=15$. The same value.

**Answer:** $x^TAx=15$ and $S=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$. Only the symmetric part counts.
cards.why_full:
Quadratic forms link matrices to optimisation: the sign of the form decides whether a point is a minimum, and the Rayleigh bounds give the maximum over the unit sphere. In GATE: evaluate $x^TAx$, find the symmetric part, find a maximum on unit vectors, or test positive definiteness (2026 DA Q65).

Asked: 2026 DA Q65

scenes.title: x = (3,1) and y = (-1,3) meet at a right angle

objects.text:
x is perpendicular
to y (90 degrees)

steps.caption: Two arrows from the origin. Draw $x=(3,1)$ and $y=(-1,3)$ from the origin.
A zero dot product means $\cos\theta=0$, so the angle is $90^\circ$ and $x\perp y$.
Length: $x^Tx=9+1=10$, so $\|x\|=\sqrt{10}\approx3.16$.
Unit vector: $u=x/\|x\|=(3,1)/\sqrt{10}\approx(0.95,\,0.32)$, which has length 1.

scenes.title: Projecting b = (2,3) onto the line through a = (3,1)

objects.text:
r is at 90 deg
to the line

steps.caption: Where does b land on the line? Draw $b=(2,3)$ and the line through $a=(3,1)$. We want the point of the line closest to $b$.
Compute $a^Tb=3\cdot2+1\cdot3=9$ and $a^Ta=9+1=10$.
Check: $a^Tr=3(-0.7)+1(2.1)=0$. The residual is perpendicular to the line, so $p$ is the closest point.

scenes.title: P keeps the line, kills the perpendicular, and P(Pb) = Pb

steps.caption: P projects onto the line through (3,1). $aa^T=[9,\, 3; 3,\, 1]$ and $a^Ta=10$, so $P=[0.9,\, 0.3; 0.3,\, 0.1]$. It is symmetric.
$Pa=(0.9\cdot3+0.3\cdot1,\ 0.3\cdot3+0.1\cdot1)=(3,1)=a$. A vector on the line stays put: eigenvalue 1.
Take $w=(-1,3)$, which is perpendicular to $a$. $Pw=(0.9(-1)+0.3\cdot3,\ 0.3(-1)+0.1\cdot3)=(0,0)$. Eigenvalue 0.
$\operatorname{tr}P=0.9+0.1=1=1+0$. The trace is the sum of the eigenvalues, so $\operatorname{tr}P=\operatorname{rank}P=1$.
$P^2=P$: for $b=(2,3)$, $Pb=(2.7,0.9)$, and projecting again gives $P(2.7,0.9)=(2.7,0.9)$. Nothing changes the second time.

scenes.title: An idempotent matrix can project along a slant

steps.caption: A has A*A = A. Test $A^2=A$ by multiplying $A$ by itself.
The second row is $-\tfrac12$ of the first, so $\operatorname{rank}A=1$, and $\operatorname{tr}A=2-1=1$. The eigenvalues are 1 and 0.
$A^T\ne A$, since $A_{12}=2$ but $A_{21}=-1$. So it is not an orthogonal projection. For example, $Ae_1=(2,-1)$.
The leftover $e_1-Ae_1=(-1,1)$ is sent to 0 by $A$. But $(2,-1)\cdot(-1,1)=-3\ne0$, so the leftover is not perpendicular to the image: this is an oblique projection.

scenes.title: b splits into a piece in U and a piece in the perpendicular line

steps.caption: U is the line through (1,2). Project: $a^Tb=1\cdot3+2\cdot1=5$ and $a^Ta=1+4=5$, so $Pb=1\cdot a=(1,2)$.
The leftover is $(I-P)b=b-Pb=(3,1)-(1,2)=(2,-1)$.
Check that it is perpendicular to $a$: $a\cdot(2,-1)=2-2=0$. So the leftover lies in $U^\perp$.
So $b=(1,2)+(2,-1)$: one piece in $U$ and one in $U^\perp$. Together they rebuild $b$.
$P$ sends all of $U^\perp$ to 0, so $\ker P=U^\perp=\operatorname{span}(2,-1)$ and $\dim\ker P=2-1=1$.

scenes.title: Normal equations: A^T A x = A^T b, then p = A x

steps.caption: A has two columns. The columns are $(1,1,0)$ and $(0,1,1)$. We want $p=Ax$ with $b-Ax$ perpendicular to both columns.
$A^TA=[2,\, 1; 1,\, 2]$, the dot products of the columns.
$A^Tb=[1\cdot3+1\cdot0+0\cdot3; 0\cdot3+1\cdot0+1\cdot3]=[3; 3]$.
Check: $r=b-p=(2,-2,2)$ and $A^Tr=(2-2,\ -2+2)=(0,0)$. The residual is perpendicular to both columns.

scenes.title: A rotation keeps lengths: x = (5,0) turns into Qx = (3,4)

steps.caption: Q has unit, perpendicular columns. The columns are $q_1=(0.6,0.8)$ and $q_2=(-0.8,0.6)$. Each has length $\sqrt{0.36+0.64}=1$, and $q_1\cdot q_2=-0.48+0.48=0$.
So $Q^TQ=I$ and $Q$ is orthogonal.
Lengths: $\|x\|=5$ and $\|Qx\|=\sqrt{9+16}=5$. Unchanged.
$\det Q=0.6\cdot0.6-(-0.8)(0.8)=0.36+0.64=1$, so $Q$ is a rotation. A reflection would have $\det=-1$.

scenes.title: Block triangular: det M = det A times det D

steps.caption: A 4x4 matrix in four blocks. Split $M$ into $2\times2$ blocks: $A=[2,\, 1; 1,\, 3]$ top-left, $B=[5,\, 6; 7,\, 8]$ top-right, a zero block bottom-left, and $D=[1,\, 2; 0,\, 3]$ bottom-right.
The zero block below the diagonal makes $M$ block upper triangular.
$\det A=2\cdot3-1\cdot1=5$.
$\det D=1\cdot3-2\cdot0=3$.
$\det M=\det A\cdot\det D=5\cdot3=15$. The block $B$ plays no part.

scenes.title: The form only sees the symmetric part of A

steps.caption: A is not symmetric. Multiply out: $x^TAx=1\cdot x_1^2+4\,x_1x_2+0\cdot x_2x_1+3\,x_2^2=x_1^2+4x_1x_2+3x_2^2$.
The cross term $4x_1x_2$ comes from both off-diagonal entries together: $4+0$.
Split it evenly: $S=\tfrac{A+A^T}{2}=[1,\, 2; 2,\, 3]$. Its cross terms are $2x_1x_2+2x_2x_1=4x_1x_2$.
$x^TSx$ at $(2,1)$: $1\cdot4+2\cdot2\cdot(2\cdot1)+3\cdot1=4+8+3=15$. The same value.
